extracted.intended_audience: law students, academics, regulators, and the informed public interested in regulatory policy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative standards for federal rulemaking and for submitting effective public comments—covering clarity, evidence, cost‑benefit balancing, interagency consensus, and use of behavioral insights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of regulations
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sunstein emphasizes transparency as a core feature of good regulation; transparency enables public participation and accountability. The Jan. 18, 2011 executive order strengthened public participation and brought rulemaking into the electronic age to improve transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and well-written rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules must be written clearly and well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OIRA worked with agencies to ensure rules were written clearly. Clear writing makes rules more usable and enforceable; Sunstein notes OIRA's role in improving clarity as part of finalizing rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence-based decisionmaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory decisions should be grounded in evidence, data, and statistical analysis rather than intuition or anecdote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sunstein's 'lodestar' is facts and human consequences measured with cost‑benefit analysis. He advocates bringing policy from anecdote to empirical analysis based on how people actually behave.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance costs and benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: OIRA is charged with balancing a new rule's costs and benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisionmakers should weigh monetary costs against expected benefits (including lives saved and illnesses prevented). Sunstein notes the Obama administration aimed to keep the numbers and cost of rules down while achieving safety and health gains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of nonquantifiable impacts (fairness, equity, dignity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations should account for hard‑to‑measure impacts on fairness, equity, and human dignity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: President Obama called for regulations to account for nonquantifiable impacts; Sunstein cites the CDC decision on HIV‑positive entry as an example where humanitarian, distributional and international benefits are difficult to monetize but must be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of cost‑benefit analysis and human consequences as lodestar
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts and human consequences, measured with cost‑benefit analysis, should guide regulatory choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sunstein calls these considerations his 'lodestar'—they should structure arguments and rule design rather than mere intuition. Cost‑benefit analysis is used both to quantify impacts and to inform tradeoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strengthened public participation and electronic commenting
rubrics_metrics.description: Public participation should be meaningful and enabled electronically to facilitate dialogue and wider input.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 2011 executive order strengthened public participation and 'brought rulemaking into the electronic age,' allowing comments to be transmitted electronically and commentators to be in dialogue with one another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of public comments: facts, evidence, and argument
rubrics_metrics.description: The best public comments are not mere opinions but contain facts, evidence, and are built around an argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sunstein advises that comments should include factual support and reasoned argumentation; comments that are only intuition or opinion are less useful. Public comment helps temper and shape rules before finalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interagency consensus and OIRA's convening role
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules should be informed by a workable consensus among relevant federal agencies, with OIRA serving as convener and information aggregator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sunstein describes OIRA's role in aggregating information and convening agencies with expertise to achieve a consensus on proposed rules; mastering program details and focusing on merits help get things right despite political pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use flexible approaches and scientific integrity; periodic 'lookback'
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulemaking should employ flexible approaches, maintain scientific integrity, and include lookbacks at existing regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Jan. 18, 2011 executive order called for cost‑benefit analysis, flexible approaches, scientific integrity, and a 'lookback' at regulation on the books—procedural features meant to improve quality and adaptability of rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final shaping of rules through public comment
rubrics_metrics.description: The final tempering of a rule should come from shaping it on the anvil of public comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sunstein notes that within the administration public input was taken very seriously and that public comment rounds materially affect the final content of regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate behavioral science and choice architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations can use behavioral economics—'choice architecture'—to nudge people toward better choices while preserving freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sunstein advocates using empirically grounded behavioral insights (e.g., replacing the food pyramid with the food plate) to design user‑friendly rules that achieve public‑policy goals without coercion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design regulations to be user‑friendly (practical and implementable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory design should emphasize usability—rules should be as user‑friendly as consumer products where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In 'Simpler' Sunstein reimagines government as user‑friendly as an iPad: rules should be based on evidence and have built‑in features that make compliance and understanding easier for the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider distributional, humanitarian, and international effects even if hard to monetize
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should evaluate distributional, humanitarian, and international consequences of rules, despite measurement challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sunstein's CDC example (lifting entry ban for HIV‑positive people) illustrates that civil‑rights and humanitarian considerations may justify rules even when benefits resist easy monetization; such effects should still inform decisionmaking.
